Oil and gas producers are back in the spotlight as Europe’s monthly petroleum import bill is now €10b higher than in 2025. Expensive fuel sharpens the focus on companies that find, extract, and process energy. That cost squeeze can reshape cash flows, capital plans, and investor attention. This article breaks down three large US listed oil and gas stocks from our screener and what to watch in each. The stocks below are just a starting sample, and the full screen surfaced 32 more oil and gas companies with equally compelling narratives that are not covered here. To identify potential high conviction ideas that match your risk profile, head straight into the Oil and Gas screener. Overview: Chevron is an integrated energy group that primarily explores for, produces, and transports crude oil and natural gas, alongside refining and chemicals businesses. Operations: Chevron generates most of its revenue from its Upstream units in the United States and internationally at about US$52b each, and its larger Downstream activities that deliver roughly US$79b internationally and US$82b in the United States. Chevron matters for this Oil and Gas screener because its Upstream wells, pipelines, and LNG projects still anchor the investment story, and the latest expansion plans highlight how management is trying to turn that footprint into long term cash generation. "Record production growth, especially in the Permian and from the Hess acquisition in areas such as Guyana and the Bakken, now sits on top of capital and drilling programs that aim to keep Permian volumes around 1 million barrels per day with lower CapEx per barrel, which supports future revenue and free cash flow." What really moves the needle for Chevron from here is how one evolving cost and volume assumption filters through to future margins. When those margin assumptions start to shift, the full narrative for Chevron shows how Chevron’s capital choices could accelerate or stall that cash engine beyond headline production targets. Overview: Range Resources focuses on producing and selling natural gas and NGLs from long life shale assets in the Appalachian region. Range Resources matters in this Oil and Gas screen because it is a pure play on US shale gas, tightly linked to Marcellus and Utica output, and its long inventory life connects directly to how investors think about future supply into power and LNG demand. What really matters now is how one emerging source of demand pressure interacts with cost discipline to shape future cash generation. That tension between demand pressure and disciplined spending is exactly what the full narrative for Range Resources unpacks. It shows where Range Resources could be accelerating or stalling beneath the headline volumes. Overview: ExxonMobil Holdings is a global energy group that primarily explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas, then sells fuels, chemicals, and specialty products under the Exxon, Esso, and Mobil brands. Operations: Most revenue comes from Energy Products at about US$334b, with sizeable Upstream oil and gas operations around US$112b across US and international markets. ExxonMobil Holdings belongs in an Oil and Gas screen because its Upstream drilling program and global fuels network still define the investment story, even as chemicals and lower emission projects add supporting income streams around the edges. "Strong production growth from high return assets in Guyana and the Permian Basin remains central, with upstream volumes outside the Middle East at the highest level in more than two decades and the Permian at over 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels per day, which supports future revenue and earnings per barrel." What really matters now is how one evolving cost and execution assumption shapes future margins and the headroom for ExxonMobil’s shareholder payouts. That trade off is exactly what the full narrative for ExxonMobil Holdings unpacks, showing where ExxonMobil Holdings may be accelerating, stalling, or quietly decoupling cash generation from headline volumes. Because that report had not been published at the time of writing, this article leans on the most recent full set of company figures, the second quarter release issued on July thirty-first, and on a pair of September newsroom items about the balance sheet. This report is part of our Oil and Gas Stocks coverage. The second quarter release, dated July thirty-first, showed earnings under American accounting rules of about fourteen and a half billion dollars, or three dollars and forty-eight cents a share. Adjusted earnings, which strip out identified items, were about fourteen point seven billion dollars, or three dollars and fifty-two cents a share. For the first quarter, by comparison, earnings were roughly four point two billion dollars, so the second quarter was a large step up. The company reports through four main segments. Upstream finds and produces crude oil and natural gas, with large positions in the Permian Basin of Texas and New Mexico, offshore Guyana, and liquefied natural gas projects abroad. Energy Products covers refining and the sale of fuels such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. Chemical Products makes the building blocks used in plastics, packaging and industrial materials. Specialty Products includes lubricants, basestocks and other higher-value items marketed under well-known brands. Upstream production in the second quarter averaged about four point five million oil-equivalent barrels a day, a little below the first quarter. The company temporarily lost roughly ten percent of its upstream output in the quarter because of the Middle East conflict, according to the Trefis summary of the July call. Seeing the image of his daughter in sexy clothes, Mr. Do was shocked and demanded to call Tram home immediately. Before her father's anger, Tram burst into tears because of self-pity: "Dad makes me feel like a child who is loved so much, but why is it still not good enough. When I was a child, I thought I was not well-behaved, when I grew up, I thought it was because I was not good, I lived not like what Dad wanted. When I was ridiculed and cursed by people, I didn't dare to call Dad, not because I didn't need protection from my family, but I was afraid that my own family would attack me. Before Tram's sincere words, Mr. Do could only silently look at the phone screen. Perhaps at this moment, he himself regretted what his daughter had to go through. In the rented room area, everyone is also discussing Tram's story. Neighbors also think that her father interfered too deeply in Tram's life. "My point of view is that children do not force anything, they can do whatever they want as long as they do not violate the law.  heads into the final days of October with a dated event on the calendar. According to the company's company website release, the energy major will publish quarterly financial results in October, and management will discuss them on a live call that begins in the morning Central time. The release followed the usual pattern, with the announcement made weeks before the report. Exxon Mobil is among the companies tracked in our Oil and Gas Stocks coverage. The timing matters because Exxon Mobil is among the largest components of the S&P 500, so its quarterly update often sets the tone for the rest of the energy group. Exxon Mobil shares trade on the New York Stock Exchange and are tracked by the S&P 500, NYSE Composite and Russell 1000. Reports from Stock Titan, Defense World and Yahoo Finance all pointed to the same date, and a preview on Yahoo Finance framed the report as a test of how the company's different businesses performed together. This article lays out what is known and what is not. It separates the confirmed schedule from outside expectations, describes the business segments that will be reported, and notes the challenges that management is likely to be asked. No results have been published yet, so no figures from the quarter are cited here. The confirmed facts are narrow but clear. In a press release posted on its company website, Exxon Mobil said it would release quarterly financial results in October. The company added that a live webcast and call would follow in the morning Central time, which is in the morning in New York. The announcement was syndicated by wire services and picked up by Stock Titan and Yahoo Finance, which is how the date reached most market participants. As is typical, the company did not preview any results in the notice. It only provided the date, the time and the instructions for listening to the webcast. Because the call comes after the release of the numbers, stock owners will have the written results first and the explanation second. That sequence often produces a step reaction, with an initial move on the headline figures and a second adjustment as management answers questions about cash flow, project timing and capital spending. Everything else in circulation, including estimates for earnings per share and revenue, comes from outside data providers rather than from Exxon Mobil. Those numbers vary by source and by the time they were compiled, which is why they are treated here as context rather than fact. Exxon Mobil reports through a handful of segments, and the quarter will show how each contributed. The upstream business produces crude oil and natural gas, and its results depend on volumes and realized prices. Energy Products, Chemical Products and Specialty Products, the downstream groupings the company has used in recent filings, depend on refining margins, chemical spreads and demand for lubricants and other specialty goods. This mix is what distinguishes the company from many exploration and production peers. When crude prices fall, refining and chemical margins can sometimes offset part of the weakness, and the reverse can also happen. The quarterly report is the moment when that internal balance becomes visible. Corporate costs and financing charges round out the picture. The company has repeatedly said that it is working to lower its structural cost base, and the quarter will show how much of that effort is appearing in reported numbers rather than in presentations. For readers following the stock, the segment table in the earnings release is usually more informative than the single headline figure. A strong total can mask weakness in part of the portfolio, and a soft total can hide a business that is moving in the right direction. Growth areas have dominated the company's communications in recent years. The first is the Permian Basin in West Texas and New Mexico, which expanded after the company completed its acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources. The second is offshore Guyana, where Exxon Mobil operates the Stabroek Block with partners and has brought several floating production vessels online. Market participants usually look for things in these regions. Is whether volumes are meeting the company's stated plans. The other is whether per-barrel costs are improving as the Permian operation is integrated and as more Guyana capacity ramps up. Both are visible in the production tables and in management commentary. Liquefied natural gas is another area to watch. The company has long-term projects under way, including a Texas export terminal in which it participates with partners, and the timing of start-up affects when volumes begin to contribute to results. Delays or early completions can shift the earnings pattern quarter to the next. The company has not said, in the materials reviewed for this article, how the quarter compares with the second on any of these measures. That comparison will arrive and it is the first thing Wall Street research desks will update in their models. Refining margins, often called crack spreads, measure the gap between the price of crude oil and the price of the fuels made from it. They tend to be strong when inventories are tight or when unplanned outages remove supply, and weak when demand softens or product stocks build. The quarter includes the end of the summer driving season, which normally supports gasoline and diesel demand. Chemicals are a different story. Margins in that business have been under pressure across the industry because of new capacity in Asia and uneven demand in construction and manufacturing. Exxon Mobil has argued that its integrated sites and its focus on higher-value products give it an advantage, and the report will show whether that claim is visible in the numbers. Planned maintenance is another variable. Refineries frequently schedule turnarounds in the shoulder months, and these can reduce throughput and raise costs for a quarter. The company usually flags such effects in its release or on the call, and they help explain why quarter looks unlike the last. None of these inputs can be read from the calendar announcement. They are described here because they are the factors that will explain the downstream line when it is published, and because they have been decisive in prior quarters according to the company's own filings. Crude oil prices have been volatile this year, moved by shifting demand expectations, decisions by large producing nations and headlines about supply routes in the Middle East. Coverage of other U.S. producers in recent weeks has referred to supply concerns around the Strait of Hormuz as factor supporting prices at times. For an integrated major, higher crude prices lift upstream earnings quickly, while the downstream businesses may face higher feedstock costs that arrive with a lag. The company has said in previous quarterly materials that it publishes sensitivity information to help readers estimate these effects, and that disclosure is useful for interpreting the quarter. Natural gas prices matter as well. A move in either direction changes line of the earnings statement, which is why the company's reconciliations of earnings by factor are closely read. Geopolitics also affects costs and logistics. Sanctions, shipping disruptions and regional conflicts can alter trade flows and insurance expenses. The company typically addresses these topics only in general terms, and market participants will listen for any change in tone. Cash allocation is a recurring theme for Exxon Mobil. The company's stated order of priorities has been to fund its capital program, support the dividend, keep a strong balance sheet and then use surplus cash for a share retirement program. How much of each it can afford depends on operating cash flow, which in turn depends on commodity prices and downstream margins. The dividend is closely watched because the company has raised it for many consecutive years, a record that stock owners regard as a signal of confidence in durable cash generation. The quarterly report is not the usual time for a dividend change, since the company has tended to announce those in other quarters, but the declaration and any commentary on the payout are part of the package. Capital spending is the other side of the ledger. Management has described a multi-year plan that emphasizes projects with strong expected economics, and it has said it will adjust the pace if conditions change. The report and call should show whether spending is tracking the plan or moving away from it. Net debt and the balance sheet round out the picture. Exxon Mobil entered recent quarters with low leverage by industry standards, and lenders will want to see that remain the case after the Pioneer deal and ongoing project spending. The energy group enters reporting season with a mixed pattern. Some pure exploration and production companies have seen their shares reach new multi-month highs in October, according to market data sites, while integrated majors have moved more modestly. The difference reflects the way each business model responds to crude oil prices. Exxon Mobil's scale gives it a different profile from smaller producers. It has a larger refining and chemical system, a bigger project pipeline and a balance sheet built to carry through cycles. That also means that its quarterly numbers tend to change less sharply than those of a company that produces only crude oil and gas. Chevron, Shell, BP and TotalEnergies report around the same time, and comparisons across the group are common. Differences in accounting for timing effects, divestments and non-recurring items can make direct comparisons tricky, so the company's own breakdown of identified items is the safer starting point. Index funds that track the S&P 500 or the [Dow Jones Industrial Average] also own the stock, so its result feeds into the broader energy weighting even though that weighting is small next to technology. Commodity price swings are the most obvious uncertainty. A quarter that begins with level for crude oil and ends with another can leave results that look different from what a simple average would imply, especially when hedging, inventory accounting and timing effects are involved. Project execution is a second challenge. Large offshore and export projects can be delayed by weather, supply chain bottlenecks or regulatory approvals, and the company has historically been candid about adjusting timelines. Any change in start-up schedules for major developments would be a notable item in the report. Climate-related disclosure rules, state and local legal actions and changes in environmental permitting all carry costs and can affect strategy. The company discusses these in its annual and quarterly filings, and the legal proceedings section is where updates appear. Finally, demand uncertainty persists. Economic growth rates, electric vehicle adoption and efficiency gains all influence long-term consumption of oil products, and the pace of change is debated. Management commentary on demand is typically cautious, which gives balance to the more optimistic production figures. The stock has not always moved in line with the headline result. In some earlier quarters, shares rose on a beat and then faded as the call revealed higher spending or softer chemical margins. In others, a modest miss was overshadowed by strong production or a confident message about costs. Market participants therefore often focus on earnings excluding identified items, and on cash flow from operations, rather than the reported net figure. Options pricing and trading volume usually rise ahead of the report, which can amplify the first reaction. A calm market on the day does not mean the report was unimportant, only that it matched what had been built into the price. That can produce a second round of repricing depending on how the details are interpreted and on what the rest of the sector reports in the days that follow. The first item is the earnings release itself, which will include the segment table, the cash flow summary and the list of identified items. The company also files a quarterly report with the Securities and Exchange Commission, usually within days, and that document contains the legal and accounting detail. The second item is the live call in the morning Central time. Management typically walks through the quarter, discusses progress on major projects and takes questions. Comments on production growth, cost reductions and capital spending are the ones most likely to change expectations. Those updates reflect their own judgments and are not company statements, so they should be read as commentary rather than as confirmed information. Finally, the reports from other energy companies over the next weeks, including ConocoPhillips, EOG Resources and Devon Energy, will help show whether Exxon Mobil's results reflect sector-wide conditions or company-specific factors. The calendar is crowded, and the picture will fill in gradually. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) slipped over 1% in overnight trading late Tuesday as the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) cleared Amazon’s $11.5 billion Globalstar acquisition, pushing the tech giant’s satellite-to-phone ambitions forward and setting the stage for tougher competition. ASTS stock jumped 6% on Tuesday to $41.96, but shares are still down 29% for the month. The FCC’s Space Bureau approved the transaction on Tuesday, including the transfer of 25 megahertz of Globalstar’s internationally harmonized mobile-satellite spectrum.  “This will enhance Amazon’s offering of direct-to-device (D2D) services, which will mean even more competition, coverage, and capacity,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said on X. The deal will pair Amazon Leo’s satellite-building capabilities, launch arrangements and ground infrastructure with Globalstar’s existing network and spectrum. The spectrum is key to Amazon’s satellite-to-phone ambitions. In its approval order, the FCC said Amazon has applied to operate a global direct-to-device system but would lack the mobile-satellite spectrum needed to run it without the acquisition. Amazon plans to use Globalstar’s assets to expand capacity and bring more services to areas beyond cellular coverage. The FCC said the deal could help close coverage gaps, boost emergency communications and improve data services for businesses and industrial users. “By approving this deal, the FCC has empowered Amazon Leo to deliver fast, next-gen satellite broadband services, increase competition, and help communities stay connected all across the country,” Carr said in the announcement. The FCC’s review also highlights how the deal could strengthen a rival to AST SpaceMobile. In its approval order, the agency cited arguments from Public Knowledge and New America’s Open Technology Institute that combining Amazon’s resources with Globalstar’s assets could create a stronger competitor to SpaceX and T-Mobile’s satellite offering, as well as AST’s partnership with AT&T. The order also notes AST’s ties with Verizon and FirstNet. AST already has FCC authorization to deploy and operate up to 248 satellites, connecting directly to standard smartphones using 700 MHz and 800 MHz spectrum in coordination with AT&T, Verizon and FirstNet. Its commercial agreement with AT&T, announced in 2024, runs through 2030. AST also signed a definitive agreement with Verizon last year. Amazon is targeting a similar opportunity: helping mobile carriers extend voice, text and data services beyond the reach of cellular towers. The company plans to begin deploying its next-generation satellite-to-device system in 2028. The deal would bring Amazon an established Apple relationship, with Globalstar already supporting emergency messaging and location sharing on compatible iPhones and Apple Watches. Amazon and Apple have agreed to maintain those services and develop future satellite features through Amazon Leo. Amazon also aims to expand beyond Globalstar’s current offerings to serve more carriers and device makers. The acquisition is expected to close in 2027, subject to remaining conditions, including replacement-satellite milestones. Amazon’s separate application for its direct-to-device system remains pending. After closing, it could also use Globalstar’s U.S. market-access approval for the planned 48-satellite C-3 network. Meanwhile, the FCC’s meeting on Thursday could advance a spectrum auction and proposals to open 500 megahertz of additional spectrum for uses including satellite-to-device services. title: Why Did XOM, BTE, VTRS Jump To 52-Week Highs Today? - TradingView
content: Shares of ExxonMobil Corp. (XOM), Baytex Energy Corp. (BTE) and Viatris Inc. (VTRS) soared to 52-week highs amid rising energy prices and Wall Street optimism. XOM stock jumped to an annual high in regular trading hours before closing 2.5% lower. BTE stock also rose to a 52-week high during market session but ended the day nearly 2% down. VTRS stock closed more than 2% higher after Piper Sandler raised its price target. XOM stock rose to a 52-week high of $184.88 as the company headed into a fourth consecutive month of gains. The energy company has been rising amid rising oil prices that have bolstered its stock. Last week, Brent crude oil prices surged to a six-month high, crossing $116 a barrel. While prices have pulled back from those levels, oil continues to edge higher as of press time. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around XOM stock was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing. The company's shares have gained 52.5% in 2026. BTE stock climbed to a 52-week high of $5.61 on Tuesday, putting it on track for its best month since November last year. Rising oil prices have also helped the company. Meanwhile, Jefferies analyst Sam Burwell initiated coverage of Baytex Energy with a ‘Buy’ rating and a C$9 ($6.40) price target. The analyst said the company sold its Eagle Ford asset at a solid price and now has net cash on its balance sheet. Jefferies finds BTE's relative valuation "compelling," adding that its growth runway should allow for the shares to re-rate higher. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTE stock dipped from ‘bullish’ to ‘neutral’ over 24 hours. The company's shares have soared nearly 70% this year. VTRS stock jumped to an annual high of $18.83 on Tuesday, putting it on track for a second consecutive month of gains. The company’s stock has risen recently on strong financial performance, raised full-year guidance, major strategic acquisitions, FDA approvals, and Wall Street optimism. Earlier this week, Piper Sandler analyst David Amsellem raised Viatris's price target to $14 from $13 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating on the shares while reviewing the third-quarter cycle for mid-to-large-cap commercial-stage biopharma companies. The analyst said that, at a high level, the multiple expansion for large caps is justified, adding that this kind of expansion should flow more to the "smaller of the larger caps." On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around VTRS stock was ‘bearish’ at the time of writing. The company's shares have gained nearly 54% year-to-date. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services.
